scenes.narration: Real data lives in files like spreadsheets and web responses. Today we read two common formats.

CSV is rows of values separated by commas; 2. csv.DictReader reads each row as a dictionary; 3. json.dumps makes text and json.loads reads it back) and an analogy card: a spreadsheet and a packing list: CSV is rows and columns, JSON is labelled boxes inside boxes
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: CSV means comma separated values. Each line is a row, and the first line names the columns. The csv module reads each row as a dictionary. JSON is the format of the web. It looks like Python dictionaries and lists. Json dumps turns Python data into JSON text. Json loads turns JSON text back into Python data. One catch. JSON keys are always strings, so a number key comes back as text.

[HL 4] Pick the fields by column name. Asha, eighty eight. Ravi, ninety two. Notice that every value is a string. Convert with int if you need numbers.

scenes.onScreen: A CSV table with a header row; each data row becomes a dictionary with the header names as keys
scenes.animation: Table rows slide out one by one and turn into dictionaries with keys from the header
scenes.narration: Look at how DictReader works. The first line is the header, name and marks. For each later line, it builds a dictionary. The header names become the keys, and the cells become the values. So a row becomes a dictionary with name and marks. Every value is a string, because a file has no way to know what is a number.

scenes.onScreen: jsondemo.py: dumps, loads, and what changes on the way

[HL 4] The text uses double quotes, and a lowercase true. [HL 5] Loads turns the text back into Python data. [HL 6] The second mark is ninety two. [HL 7] And now the catch. A dictionary with the number one as a key, after a round trip, is not equal to the original. False. The key came back as the text one.

code.source:
import json
data = {"name": "Asha", "marks": [88, 92], "pass": True}
text = json.dumps(data)
print(text)
back = json.loads(text)
print(back["marks"][1])
print({1: "a"} == json.loads(json.dumps({1: "a"})))

bug.error:
Python output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

{'1': 'one'}
bug.fixed:
import json
data = {1: "one"}
back = json.loads(json.dumps(data))
print({int(k): v for k, v in back.items()})
bug.why: JSON only allows string keys, so a number key is written as text; convert the keys back yourself after loading.

shorts.title: CSV files
shorts.hook: "A CSV file stores a table as plain text."
shorts.script: A CSV file stores a table as plain text. Each line is a row, and the cells are separated by commas. The first line names the columns. The csv module can read each row as a dictionary, keyed by those names. Use DictReader, and pick fields like row, bracket, name. Every value arrives as a string, so convert numbers with int. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Spreadsheets as text.

shorts.title: DictReader
shorts.hook: "Csv dot DictReader reads a file, and gives you one dictionary for each data row."
shorts.script: Csv dot DictReader reads a file, and gives you one dictionary for each data row. The first line becomes the keys. So you write row name, and row marks, and the code reads like the table. It is far safer than splitting lines by commas yourself, because it handles quotes, and commas inside cells. Open the file with with, and loop. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A dictionary per row.

shorts.title: JSON text
shorts.hook: "JSON is the format of the web."
shorts.script: JSON is the format of the web. It looks like Python dictionaries and lists. Json dumps turns Python data into JSON text, ready to save or send. Json loads turns JSON text back into Python data. Together they let your program talk to files, and to other programs, in a format that almost every language understands. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Python data to text and back.

shorts.title: Keys become strings
shorts.script: A small JSON surprise. You save a dictionary with the number one as a key. You load it back, and the key is now the text one. JSON only allows string keys. A lookup with the number one fails. After loading, convert the keys back with int, in a dictionary comprehension, and your data is whole again. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: JSON keys are text.

codeFiles.source:
import csv
with open("marks.csv") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["name"], row["marks"])

import json
data = {"name": "Asha", "marks": [88, 92], "pass": True}
text = json.dumps(data)
print(text)
back = json.loads(text)
print(back["marks"][1])
print({1: "a"} == json.loads(json.dumps({1: "a"})))
